# Morris Park Aerodrome

Morris Park Aerodrome was an early aviation venue established in 1908 on the grounds of the former Morris Park Racecourse in the East Bronx, New York City , . It holds the distinction of being recognized as the world's first formally established airport or airfield, marking a significant transition from informal flight demonstrations to organized aviation hubs , . The aerodrome served as a crucial proving ground for pioneering aircraft and hosted some of the earliest public air shows in the United States, including the world's first public air meet held in November 1908 , . Operated by the newly formed Aeronautic Society of New York (ASN), the site became a focal point for public fascination with flight, attracting prominent aviators like Glenn H. Curtiss, who conducted high-profile exhibition flights there in June 1909 , . Despite its foundational importance, the aerodrome's operational life was remarkably brief. After a flurry of activity in 1908 and 1909, the ASN's lease expired, and the property was sold at auction in 1913 . The land was subsequently redeveloped for urban use, with its function superseded by later airports such as Floyd Bennett Field . The site itself was later repurposed again for another aviation-related project in 1927, demonstrating a recurring pattern of aviation interest in this specific parcel of land .

## Genesis and Establishment

The establishment of Morris Park Aerodrome was a direct consequence of the rapid technological advancements in aviation at the turn of the 20th century and the repurposing of existing large-scale infrastructure to accommodate them. The site itself was not new; it was the location of the Morris Park Racecourse, a major horse racing facility constructed in 1889 , . The racecourse, which opened as the "finest race track in the world," featured a 1½-mile main track, a ¾-mile diagonal Eclipse track, a grandstand accommodating 15,000 spectators, and extensive stabling facilities . It was a prominent venue in American thoroughbred racing, hosting the prestigious Belmont Stakes from 1890 until 1904, as well as the Preakness Stakes in 1890 . However, due to declining attendance and membership, coupled with the imminent opening of the larger Belmont Park nearby, the Westchester Racing Association, which owned the track, held its final day of races on October 15, 1904 . This left a vast, open, and unobstructed expanse of land ideally suited for the nascent field of heavier-than-air flight.

Following the closure of the racetrack, the City of New York assumed control of the property in 1907 . Recognizing the potential of the space, the city entered into a lease agreement with the recently formed Aeronautic Society of New York (ASN) . The ASN was established in 1908 as a breakaway group from the Aero Club of America, comprising influential members dissatisfied with the parent club's direction . The society's stated mission was the practical pursuit of mechanical flight, and it quickly distinguished itself as a proactive organization dedicated to creating the necessary infrastructure for this pursuit . One of its very first official acts was to lease the 372-acre (151 ha) property of the defunct Morris Park Racetrack and dedicate it as a formal flying ground , . This act effectively transformed the abandoned racetrack into the world's first officially designated airport , . While the ASN was chartered on June 10, 1908, coinciding with the opening of the aerodrome, the lease agreement itself solidified the site's status as a permanent hub for aviation in the region . The ASN was described by chronicler Edward Tandy as "the first organization the world formed for the practical pursuit of the problem of mechanical flight by man," the first to have dedicated flying grounds, and the first to hold public exhibitions . The transformation of the racetrack involved removing fences to create an unobstructed straightway suitable for flights of at least one kilometer, a critical requirement for the experimental aircraft of the era . This strategic repurposing of a major civic asset underscored the growing cultural and technological importance of aviation in early 20th-century New York.

## Events and Activities

Morris Park Aerodrome quickly fulfilled its role as a central venue for early American aviation, serving as a dynamic laboratory for experimentation and a spectacular stage for public demonstrations. Its most celebrated event was the world's first public air meet, held on November 3, 1908, before an estimated crowd of 20,000 spectators . This inaugural exhibition showcased the diverse and often radical ideas being explored by aviation pioneers. Among the featured aircraft was William Kimball’s 20-rotor helicopter, also referred to as a 'heliocopter', which Wilbur H. Kimbull had assembled and tested at the aerodrome in early September 1908 , . Another remarkable device was the Rickman Helicopter, a contraption with 32 propellers powered by two men pedaling a tandem bicycle . While none of the experimental craft achieved sustained, controlled powered flight during the meet, wind-powered gliders did manage to fly successfully . Canadian teenager Laurence Jerome Lesh exhibited his glider, which was designed to be towed aloft by two automobiles connected by a long rope . His exhibition included several successful flights, but also a spectacular crash landing that resulted in him breaking his ankle, highlighting the inherent dangers and learning curve of early aviation , . The aerodrome continued to be a hub of activity just two days later, on November 5, 1908, when Lesh and other exhibitors presented a series of gliding exhibitions, demonstrating the site's role as a continuous proving ground for new technologies .

The aerodrome's reputation for hosting significant aviation events was cemented by the arrival of Glenn H. Curtiss, one of the leading figures in American aviation. In June 1909, Curtiss conducted a series of exhibition flights at Morris Park that were described by The New York Times as having "seized the imagination of the nation’s largest city" , . These performances were not merely technical displays but strategic publicity moves designed to popularize flight and attract investors and customers . Curtiss's success at Morris Park preceded his July 1909 victory in winning the Scientific American Trophy for a flight of nearly twenty-five miles, confirming the site's role as a key venue for his high-profile promotional efforts . The aerodrome's operational status was further validated by a landmark transaction in June 1909, when the Aeronautic Society of New York purchased Glenn Curtiss's No. 1 airplane for $7,500 . This acquisition gave the ASN its own powered aircraft, moving it from simply providing a venue to actively operating aircraft, and directly linked the aerodrome to the core of the burgeoning American aviation industry . This sale also triggered the Wright brothers' patent lawsuit against Curtiss, a legal battle that would have profound implications for the entire industry . The aerodrome remained a center for ambitious projects through late 1909. On October 10, 1909, The New York Times reported that two Arkansas men, Joel T. Rice and John A. Riggs, were completing the construction of what was billed as the largest dirigible balloon ever built in America at Morris Park, with plans to launch it from the site , . This confirmed that the aerodrome was still a functioning and relevant aviation site at least two years after its initial establishment, contradicting assumptions that it had ceased operations by 1910 .

## Key Personnel and Aircraft

The history of Morris Park Aerodrome is inseparable from the stories of the visionary individuals and their unconventional aircraft who brought the dream of flight to life. At the forefront of the aerodrome's establishment was the Aeronautic Society of New York (ASN), a group of passionate enthusiasts and investors who provided the organizational and financial backbone for early aviation in the region . Formed in 1908 by members disillusioned with the Aero Club of America, the ASN immediately demonstrated its commitment by securing the lease for the Morris Park Racecourse and establishing it as the world's first dedicated flying grounds , . The society's leadership included figures like Lee Burridge, Albert Triaca, Willard Kimball, Roger Whitman, and Stanley Beach, all of whom were instrumental in chartering the society and setting up the aerodrome . Their actions, particularly the purchase of Glenn Curtiss's No. 1 airplane in June 1909, were pivotal moments that cemented the aerodrome's operational status and placed it at the heart of the national aviation scene .

Glenn H. Curtiss was arguably the most influential figure to operate at Morris Park Aerodrome. As both an inventor and a master showman, his presence and exhibitions in June 1909 were transformative . His aircraft represented the cutting edge of technology, and his ability to perform complex maneuvers captivated audiences and convinced skeptics of the viability of heavier-than-air flight . The sale of his No. 1 airplane to the ASN was a landmark event, symbolizing the shift from individual experimentation to institutional investment in aviation . This transaction not only provided the ASN with its first powered aircraft but also thrust Curtiss into the center of a major legal dispute with the Wright brothers over patent infringement, a conflict that would define the American aviation industry for decades . Other key personnel included the inventors themselves. Wilbur H. Kimbull, for instance, was testing his innovative "heliocopter"—a machine with 20 rotors—on the aerodrome grounds in September 1908, showcasing an early attempt at vertical lift technology . Canadian teenager Laurence Jerome Lesh arrived at the aerodrome in late 1908 with his glider, demonstrating a novel method of launching by towing the craft with two automobiles . His participation in the November air meets, culminating in a dramatic crash that broke his ankle, exemplified the risks and hands-on nature of early flight testing , .

The aircraft that operated at Morris Park Aerodrome provide a fascinating snapshot of the technological diversity of the era. The site was less about refined, commercially viable machines and more of a crucible for radical innovation. Kimball's "heliocopter" stands out as a pioneering effort in vertical flight, while the Rickman Helicopter, with its 32 propellers driven by human power, represents an imaginative solution to the problem of propulsion . Lesh's glider, though reliant on automobile power for launch, was a sophisticated piece of engineering for soaring flight . Perhaps the most ambitious project undertaken at the aerodrome was the dirigible built by Joel T. Rice and John A. Riggs in 1909 . This airship was unlike any seen before in America; it featured a lightweight steel frame, a powerful 34-hp Curtiss eight-cylinder motor, dual side propellers for altitude control, and a novel front-propeller-as-rudder steering system patented by Rice . The sheer scale of the project—a cotton envelope with a capacity of over 35,000 cubic feet—indicates that Morris Park Aerodrome was a venue for serious, large-scale aeronautical engineering, not just fleeting public demonstrations .

## Legacy and Demise

The legacy of Morris Park Aerodrome is defined by its foundational role in the history of aviation and the remarkable brevity of its existence. As the world's first officially established airport, it set a precedent for the development of organized airfields globally, transitioning aviation from isolated experiments into a structured public spectacle , . Its influence extended beyond its physical footprint, shaping the trajectory of American aviation through its association with the Aeronautic Society of New York and its connection to the legal battles over patents between Curtiss and the Wright brothers . The aerodrome served as a vital incubator for new ideas and technologies, from vertical-flight concepts to large-scale dirigibles, contributing to the collective knowledge base of early flight , . However, this period of pioneering activity was intensely concentrated and ultimately ephemeral. The Aeronautic Society of New York's lease on the 372-acre site came to an end, and the property was put up for sale by the City of New York in 1913 . By 1916, the aerodrome had been completely torn down to make way for urban development, its function superseded by newer, more modern airports like Floyd Bennett Field in Brooklyn , . The site, once the epicenter of public fascination with flight, was absorbed into the expanding cityscape of the Bronx .

Despite the disappearance of the original aerodrome, the land maintained a unique connection to aviation history. Decades after the ASN vacated the premises, the general area was chosen again for an aviation venture. In August 1927, a new airfield was established on a marshy tract in the Bronx by local businessmen, with the Bronx Chamber of Commerce playing a key role . This second iteration of an airport on the site underscores a persistent desire within the borough to establish its own aviation hub. However, this endeavor also proved to be short-lived. The inaugural landing at the new airfield ended in a crash when a biplane struck an unattended car on the makeshift runway . Although the project was intended to become part of a nationwide chain of airports developed by the Curtiss-Wright corporation, the chain stalled following the stock market crash of October 1929 . The airfield remained largely undeveloped throughout the Great Depression and was finally abandoned after World War II. The land was eventually sold to a developer who constructed Co-op City, the nation's largest residential cooperative development, erasing the final traces of aviation from the landscape . The story of Morris Park Aerodrome thus serves as a poignant example of the transience of early aviation infrastructure and the relentless pace of urbanization in 20th-century New York. The aerodrome itself has been noted as a potential candidate for listing on the National Register of Historic Places, though definitive documentation for such a listing is not available in the provided sources .

## Location and Historical Context

Morris Park Aerodrome was situated in the East Bronx, New York City, occupying the expansive grounds of the former Morris Park Racecourse , . Its precise geographical boundaries were defined by Sackett Avenue to the south, the Amtrak Northeast Corridor railroad right-of-way to the east, Bronxdale Road to the west, and Pelham Parkway to the north . The site was bounded on the east by Williamsbridge Road prior to its aviation conversion . The grandstand of the old racetrack stood at the intersection of Bogart and Fowler Avenues, and the clubhouse was near the intersection of Fowler and Van Nest Avenues, providing key reference points for the layout of the ASN's leasehold . The aerodrome's location was strategically advantageous, offering a large, flat, and unobstructed area ideal for the takeoff and landing of early, often unstable, aircraft . The neighborhood of Morris Park, which surrounds the area today, is defined by Neill Avenue and Pelham Parkway to the north, Eastchester Road to the east, and Bronxdale Avenue or White Plains Road to the west, placing the historic aerodrome firmly within the modern urban fabric of the Bronx .

The historical context of the aerodrome's establishment is deeply rooted in the history of the Bronx itself. The land was part of the Morrisania estate, originally owned by colonial-era figures Gouverneur Morris and his half-brother Lewis Morris . The estate was divided by Mill Brook, which is now the site of St. Mary's Park, indicating a long history of land division and development in the area . The construction of the Morris Park Racecourse in the late 19th century represented a period of major investment and development in the region, transforming Bear Swamp into a premier sporting venue . The subsequent decline and abandonment of the racecourse mirrored broader economic shifts, paving the way for the next wave of technological change. The leasing of the property to the Aeronautic Society of New York in 1907 was a municipal decision that reflected the city's forward-looking attitude toward emerging technologies . The aerodrome was not an isolated phenomenon but rather a product of its time, born from the convergence of a vacant, underutilized space and a burgeoning public and private enthusiasm for flight. The fact that the ASN could acquire such a large parcel of land for aviation purposes highlights the experimental and opportunistic nature of the early aviation community. The aerodrome's story is therefore intertwined with the history of urban planning, real estate development, and technological innovation in New York City during the Progressive Era.

## Archival and Research Materials

A wealth of archival and cartographic materials exists to verify and expand upon the history of Morris Park Aerodrome, providing researchers with a detailed toolkit for investigating the site's location, boundaries, and evolution. The New York Public Library (NYPL) holds extensive fire insurance atlases from the early 20th century, which are critical for mapping the pre-aerodrome landscape , . Atlases published by companies like Sanborn, Bromley, and Hyde from the periods of 1901–1907 provide contemporaneous, official survey data of the Morris Park Racecourse , . These maps meticulously detail the layout of the racetrack, including the grandstand, clubhouse, stables, and surrounding streets, allowing for a precise determination of the exact parcel of land leased by the Aeronautic Society of New York , . For instance, the 1904 Bromley atlas and the 1908 Sanborn atlas would clearly show the infrastructure of the defunct racetrack, forming the baseline for understanding the aerodrome's initial setup .

To trace the aerodrome's operational phase and its eventual redevelopment, later editions of these atlases are essential. The Atlas of the Borough of the Bronx published by Bromley in 1927 provides the earliest known surveyed map covering the post-racecourse era, capturing the land status immediately before and during the establishment of the later Curtiss-Wright airfield in 1927 . This allows for a definitive spatial comparison with earlier maps, helping to distinguish the footprint of the 1908 aerodrome from the 1927 airfield . In addition to atlases, the NYC Department of Finance tax maps can show lot shapes and dimensions, while citywide photographic surveys from 1940 and the mid-1980s may capture the timing of built development against the aerodrome's closure and redevelopment phases . The Bronx County Archives (BCA) and the Bronx County Historical Society (BCHS) are key repositories for related materials . The BCA holds collections that may include municipal leases, survey maps, and aerial photographs from the early 20th century . The BCHS maintains microfilm collections of Bronx newspapers, such as the *Bronx Home News*, which could contain additional contemporary accounts of the aerodrome's events . Furthermore, the Bronx Borough President's Office archives contain street profiles, grade maps, and departmental plans that could provide further insight into the city's planning decisions regarding the land . Unprocessed collections, such as aerial photographs from circa 1920–1959 and records of land acquisition proceedings from 1930–1962, suggest that visual and documentary evidence of the site's transformation remains accessible for scholarly investigation , . These resources collectively offer a robust foundation for accurately reconstructing the history and geography of Morris Park Aerodrome.

This endeavor also proved to be short-lived.
The inaugural landing at the new airfield ended in a crash when a biplane struck an unattended car on the makeshift runway.
The project was intended to become part of a nationwide chain of airports developed by the Curtiss-Wright corporation.
The chain stalled following the stock market crash of October 1929.
The airfield remained largely undeveloped throughout the Great Depression.
The airfield was finally abandoned after World War II.
The land was eventually sold to a developer who constructed Co-op City.
Co-op City is the nation's largest residential cooperative development.
The construction of Co-op City erased the final traces of aviation from the landscape.
The story of Morris Park Aerodrome serves as a poignant example of the transience of early aviation infrastructure.
The story of Morris Park Aerodrome serves as a poignant example of the relentless pace of urbanization in 20th-century New York.
The aerodrome itself has been noted as a potential candidate for listing on the National Register of Historic Places.
Definitive documentation for a listing on the National Register of Historic Places is not available in the provided sources.
Morris Park Aerodrome was situated in the East Bronx, New York City.
Morris Park Aerodrome occupied the expansive grounds of the former Morris Park Racecourse.
Its precise geographical boundaries were defined by Sackett Avenue to the south.
Its precise geographical boundaries were defined by the Amtrak Northeast Corridor railroad right-of-way to the east.
Its precise geographical boundaries were defined by Bronxdale Road to the west.
Its precise geographical boundaries were defined by Pelham Parkway to the north.
The site was bounded on the east by Williamsbridge Road prior to its aviation conversion.
The grandstand of the old racetrack stood at the intersection of Bogart and Fowler Avenues.
The clubhouse was near the intersection of Fowler and Van Nest Avenues.
The grandstand and clubhouse provided key reference points for the layout of the ASN's leasehold.
The aerodrome's location was strategically advantageous, offering a large, flat, and unobstructed area.
The aerodrome's location was ideal for the takeoff and landing of early, often unstable, aircraft.
The neighborhood of Morris Park is defined by Neill Avenue and Pelham Parkway to the north.
The neighborhood of Morris Park is defined by Eastchester Road to the east.
The neighborhood of Morris Park is defined by Bronxdale Avenue or White Plains Road to the west.
The historic aerodrome is firmly within the modern urban fabric of the Bronx.
The historical context of the aerodrome's establishment is deeply rooted in the history of the Bronx itself.
The land was part of the Morrisania estate.
The Morrisania estate was originally owned by colonial-era figures Gouverneur Morris and his half-brother Lewis Morris.
The estate was divided by Mill Brook.
Mill Brook is now the site of St. Mary's Park.
The construction of the Morris Park Racecourse in the late 19th century represented a period of major investment and development in the region.
The construction of the Morris Park Racecourse transformed Bear Swamp into a premier sporting venue.
The subsequent decline and abandonment of the racecourse mirrored broader economic shifts.
The subsequent decline and abandonment of the racecourse paved the way for the next wave of technological change.
The leasing of the property to the Aeronautic Society of New York in 1907 was a municipal decision.
The municipal decision to lease the property to the Aeronautic Society of New York reflected the city's forward-looking attitude toward emerging technologies.
The aerodrome was a product of its time, born from the convergence of a vacant, underutilized space and a burgeoning public and private enthusiasm for flight.
The fact that the ASN could acquire such a large parcel of land for aviation purposes highlights the experimental and opportunistic nature of the early aviation community.
The aerodrome's story is intertwined with the history of urban planning, real estate development, and technological innovation in New York City during the Progressive Era.
A wealth of archival and cartographic materials exists to verify and expand upon the history of Morris Park Aerodrome.
The New York Public Library (NYPL) holds extensive fire insurance atlases from the early 20th century.
Fire insurance atlases are critical for mapping the pre-aerodrome landscape.
Atlases published by companies like Sanborn, Bromley, and Hyde from the periods of 1901–1907 provide contemporaneous, official survey data of the Morris Park Racecourse.
These maps meticulously detail the layout of the racetrack, including the grandstand, clubhouse, stables, and surrounding streets.
These maps allow for a precise determination of the exact parcel of land leased by the Aeronautic Society of New York.
The 1904 Bromley atlas and the 1908 Sanborn atlas would clearly show the infrastructure of the defunct racetrack.
The 1904 Bromley atlas and the 1908 Sanborn atlas form the baseline for understanding the aerodrome's initial setup.
Later editions of these atlases are essential to trace the aerodrome's operational phase and its eventual redevelopment.
The Atlas of the Borough of the Bronx published by Bromley in 1927 provides the earliest known surveyed map covering the post-racecourse era.
The 1927 Atlas of the Borough of the Bronx captures the land status immediately before and during the establishment of the later Curtiss-Wright airfield in 1927.
This allows for a definitive spatial comparison with earlier maps.
This helps to distinguish the footprint of the 1908 aerodrome from the 1927 airfield.
The NYC Department of Finance tax maps can show lot shapes and dimensions.
Citywide photographic surveys from 1940 and the mid-1980s may capture the timing of built development against the aerodrome's closure and redevelopment phases.
The Bronx County Archives (BCA) and the Bronx County Historical Society (BCHS) are key repositories for related materials.
The BCA holds collections that may include municipal leases, survey maps, and aerial photographs from the early 20th century.
The BCHS maintains microfilm collections of Bronx newspapers, such as the *Bronx Home News*.
Microfilm collections of Bronx newspapers could contain additional contemporary accounts of the aerodrome's events.
The Bronx Borough President's Office archives contain street profiles, grade maps, and departmental plans.
The Bronx Borough President's Office archives could provide further insight into the city's planning decisions regarding the land.
Unprocessed collections, such as aerial photographs from circa 1920–1959, suggest that visual and documentary evidence of the site's transformation remains accessible for scholarly investigation.

Unprocessed collections, such as records of land acquisition proceedings from 1930–1962, suggest that visual and documentary evidence of the site's transformation remains accessible for scholarly investigation.
These resources collectively offer a robust foundation for accurately reconstructing the history and geography of Morris Park Aerodrome.

3.content:
[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ngoF!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7b0f580b-2c96-4cef-87b9-e2a2d1d1e36d_1270x1272.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ngoF!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7b0f580b-2c96-4cef-87b9-e2a2d1d1e36d_1270x1272.jpeg)

Before I started researching Morris Park, I assumed it got its name from the Morris family, the namesake of the neighborhoods of [Port Morris](https://theneighborhoods.substack.com/p/port-morris-the-bronx) and Morrasania, also in the Bronx. However, the neighborhood is actually named in honor of horse enthusiast and “Lottery King” John Albert Morris.

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!GUJN!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb9296720-0730-4733-b2ce-b1b0ec97b46f_2000x1600.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!GUJN!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb9296720-0730-4733-b2ce-b1b0ec97b46f_2000x1600.jpeg)

Morris Park is between Pelham Parkway to the North, the Hutchinson River Parkway to the East, the Amtrak Northeast Corridor tracks to the south, and White Plains Road to the West. The neighborhood has traditionally been Italian American, though there has been a significant increase in the Albanian population in recent years.

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!uMYE!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fde598ce8-768a-418e-a081-8ea0526986f2_990x818.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!uMYE!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fde598ce8-768a-418e-a081-8ea0526986f2_990x818.jpeg)

John Morris made his fortune from the Louisiana State Lottery Company,  a venture he founded in 1868 under the pretext of raising money to fund reconstruction efforts after the Civil War.

At the time, most states had banned lotteries since they were, at best, immoral and, at worst, brazenly corrupt. For a long time, The Louisiana State Lottery Company was the only legal lottery in the US, a distinction it earned through generous bribes and influence peddling. Taking advantage of the reach of the U.S. Postal Service, the company sold lottery tickets nationwide, earning it the nickname of the Golden Octopus. It quickly became one of the largest businesses in the United States.

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!xXfq!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0ad54431-4f95-4566-9e53-37bfb1b7ac2b_616x368.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!xXfq!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0ad54431-4f95-4566-9e53-37bfb1b7ac2b_616x368.jpeg)

At its peak, the lottery was generating $2,000,000 in sales per week, a ”fountain of wealth to which that of Monte Cristo was but a mere bagatelle.” [1](https://theneighborhoods.substack.com/p/morris-park-the-bronx#footnote-1-140966467)

Finally, in 1890, Congress outlawed the mailing of any lottery-related material. Morris moved his headquarters to Honduras and rebranded as The Honduras Lottery Company. He circumvented the new postal ban by having employees collect and carry lottery tickets in their luggage. The scheme continued to operate in the shadows until 1907, when two printing presses owned by the company in Alabama and Delaware were seized, and they were forced to dissolve.

In 1889, flush with lottery money, Morris opened the Morris Park Racecourse, once described as "the finest race track in the world,” on the site of present-day Morris Park. From 1890 to 1904, the racecourse hosted the Belmont Stakes.

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!aKNp!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9b95fb57-c071-459c-95ca-0d5439eb4b0e_1916x1096.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!aKNp!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9b95fb57-c071-459c-95ca-0d5439eb4b0e_1916x1096.jpeg)

Maybe this haunted looking clubhouse kept people away

The Belmont was originally held at the Jerome racetrack, which I wrote about in my [Kingsbridge Heights](https://theneighborhoods.substack.com/p/bones-of-the-buddha-in-the-bronx) post.

[![Image 6: Crowds of people and carriages waiting to get into Morris Park Race track](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ekKz!,w_2400,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F40bd38b4-5fe7-4607-97d1-abab41ead77c_2060x707.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ekKz!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F40bd38b4-5fe7-4607-97d1-abab41ead77c_2060x707.jpeg)

Morris Park Race Track, the entrance to grandstand, B.J., Falk, 1903

The race track closed in 1904 due to declining attendance and, for a couple of years, was repurposed for automobiles, with the first-ever Indy car race held there in 1905.

Then, in 1908, the Aeronautic Society secured the lease for the 372-acre site in the Bronx, paving the way for the world’s first formal airfield.

The Aeronautic Society of New York was formed by members of The Aero Club of America, who were frustrated by the latter’s single-minded focus on hot-air ballooning. They viewed the Aero club as “dominated by a handful of elite sportsmen who had taken up ballooning, supplemented by a larger number of armchair aeronauts drawn from the cream of New York society.”[2](https://theneighborhoods.substack.com/p/morris-park-the-bronx#footnote-2-140966467)

The Aeronautic Society members wanted to focus on "heavier-than-air flight,” inspired no doubt by the well-documented successes of the Wright Brothers.

Society members set up shop in the vacant stables and barns and began to build some of the most fantastical machines ever seen.

> **Soon, the people of the neighborhood began to whisper to one another that queer-looking machines were being built up at the racetrack, and every day, curious, inquisitive little throngs would venture in and peep. Never before had the like of such things been seen in New York City!**[3](https://theneighborhoods.substack.com/p/morris-park-the-bronx#footnote-3-140966467)

Take, for example, William Kimball’s helicopter with its 20 rotors driven by an intricate system of leather belts and pulleys.

[![Image 7](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!m9kk!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8caf17bf-64ef-4605-83d5-90b1a9d1b649_1666x1255.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!m9kk!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8caf17bf-64ef-4605-83d5-90b1a9d1b649_1666x1255.png)

[![Image 8](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!GcOx!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F213e3d8e-662a-436c-9cec-af9097bd41ef_548x301.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!GcOx!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F213e3d8e-662a-436c-9cec-af9097bd41ef_548x301.jpeg)

Not to be outdone was the Rickman Helicopter, boasting 32 propellors powered by two men, possessing what must have been enormous quads, astride a tandem bicycle.

[![Image 9](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!qzgC!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbb1e3288-171b-43d7-abf1-c9492be83ae1_1024x532.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!qzgC!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbb1e3288-171b-43d7-abf1-c9492be83ae1_1024x532.jpeg)

And there was the C.W. Williams’ “weird and wonderful ” monoplane

[![Image 10](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!R77L!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb6b01372-0c72-40a1-bc13-10590622b057_1000x628.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!R77L!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb6b01372-0c72-40a1-bc13-10590622b057_1000x628.jpeg)

On November 3rd, 1908, those inventions and dozens more were put to the test in front of a crowd of 20,000 spectators.  Not a single one of them managed to get off the ground.

At least the wind-powered gliders made it airborne, though, in Lawrence Lesh’s case, he may have been better off staying put. Lesh spent seven months recovering in nearby Fordam Hospital after the crowds, excited to finally have a reason to look up, encroached upon his landing spot, forcing him into a crash landing that broke his ankle.

[![Image 11](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1es5!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F40941b03-a58b-46a6-af98-e0f0d5c01915_364x580.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1es5!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F40941b03-a58b-46a6-af98-e0f0d5c01915_364x580.jpeg)

“There is an art, it says, or rather, a knack to flying. The knack lies in learning how to throw yourself at the ground and miss. … Clearly, it is this second part, the missing, which presents the difficulties.” - Douglas Adams

These pictures reminded me more than a bit of the work of Shana and Robert ParkeHarrison. In particular, this image, The Sower:

[![Image 12](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!EEyr!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Feb9a20f8-cf88-4e8c-b504-7883277b1868_505x600.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!EEyr!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Feb9a20f8-cf88-4e8c-b504-7883277b1868_505x600.jpeg)

After a big fire at the racetrack in 1910, the city auctioned off the land to real estate developers in 1913.

[![Image 13](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ZsQU!,w_2400,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F61bdfe91-4322-4962-a17b-cd9ddcac162c_1242x939.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ZsQU!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F61bdfe91-4322-4962-a17b-cd9ddcac162c_1242x939.jpeg)

Several years ago, while working with the great musician and photographer [John Cohen](https://www.johncohenworks.com/) on his archive in the Hudson Valley, I would frequently drive by the blunt silhouette of a building slowly rising on the edge of the Hutchinson River Parkway. One day, I finally pulled over to take a picture.

[![Image 14](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1p7Y!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd12b3467-da97-4c21-b142-e2649ff1cf7a_1599x2000.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1p7Y!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd12b3467-da97-4c21-b142-e2649ff1cf7a_1599x2000.jpeg)

I love unadorned buildings, structures reduced to the simplest of geometric forms. While I can appreciate the haphazard offset stacks of [56 Leonard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/56_Leonard_Street) (the Jenga building) or the graceful concrete curves of Eero Saarinen’s TWA terminal, there is just something about a simple rectangle that feels both ancient and futuristic.

PSAC II, a 450,000-square-foot monolith, is a perfect cube, a 240-foot wide by 240-foot tall concrete block sheathed in a serrated aluminum facade. The near absence of windows is a security measure.

PSAC stands for Public Safety Answering Center. It can handle all emergency 911 calls and communications in the event that PSAC I (in the Metrotech Center in downtown Brooklyn) goes down. The building was designed to survive a natural disaster or an attack and is said to be “virtually impregnable.” Anti-ram walls and bollards surround the grounds, and the loading bays are equipped with blast doors. There are multiple generators and battery systems, along with enough food to keep the center running for days off the grid.  It is a fortress.

[![Image 15](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!NHlM!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff69888ff-0000-4578-bb5c-9ae1ffd3dc4c_2000x1600.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!NHlM!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff69888ff-0000-4578-bb5c-9ae1ffd3dc4c_2000x1600.jpeg)

The Morris Park Crew, or MPC, was a gang of graffiti “bombers” formed in the neighborhood in 1977. In the early 80s, notorious bomber Cap One took over the crew. Cap was infamous for “going over” other graffiti artists’ work, a practice that made him the public enemy of anybody not in the MPC.

[![Image 16](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!EQns!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff04c36e4-5fd8-47fa-9f73-5f25209f02e3_2000x1600.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!EQns!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff04c36e4-5fd8-47fa-9f73-5f25209f02e3_2000x1600.jpeg)

Not MPC’s work

The fantastic 1983 documentary [Style Wars](https://youtu.be/qqUwNkr-B3k?si=fao-ItZGosdDxFQT) (free on Youtube) was called the “defining documentary of early hip-hop culture" by Pitchfork (RIP). The doc features interviews with graffiti writers like Cap, Kase 2, and Skeme, whose interview alongside his mothers is one of the best parts of the film.

Other highlights include footage of the dance battle between the Rock Steady Crew and the Dynamic Rockers and a clip of Mayor Ed Koch half-seriously proposing that wolves patrol the train yards to deter would-be vandals. There is no better document of early 80s New York City culture.

**5/5** stars

[![Image 18](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!nnix!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4d2b1b1d-2c85-4647-aa79-7a0b3b2d7181_2000x1600.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!nnix!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4d2b1b1d-2c85-4647-aa79-7a0b3b2d7181_2000x1600.jpeg)

Morris Park, The Bronx
----------------------

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

**Morris Park** is a neighborhood in the [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") borough of [the Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bronx "The Bronx"). Its approximate boundaries, starting from the north and moving clockwise, are Neill Avenue and [Pelham Parkway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelham_Parkway_/(road/) "Pelham Parkway (road)") to the north, Eastchester Road to the East, the [Amtrak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amtrak "Amtrak") [Northeast Corridor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeast_Corridor "Northeast Corridor") tracks and Sackett Avenue to the east and south, and Bronxdale Avenue or [White Plains Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Plains_Road "White Plains Road") to the west. It borders the neighborhoods of [Van Nest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Nest "Van Nest") to its southwest and [Pelham Parkway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelham_Parkway_/(neighborhood/),_Bronx "Pelham Parkway (neighborhood), Bronx") to its northeast. Williamsbridge Road and Morris Park Avenue are the primary thoroughfares.

The neighborhood is part of [Bronx Community District 11](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronx_Community_Board_11 "Bronx Community Board 11") in the [East Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Bronx "East Bronx"), and its ZIP Codes include 10461 and 10462. The area is patrolled by the 49th Precinct of the [New York City Police Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Police_Department "New York City Police Department"), located at 2121 Eastchester Road. The local subway is the [IRT Dyre Avenue Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IRT_Dyre_Avenue_Line "IRT Dyre Avenue Line") ([5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5_/(New_York_City_Subway_service/) "5 (New York City Subway service)") train), which runs under the Esplanade. The neighborhood has a large [Albanian American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albanian_American "Albanian American") and [Italian American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_American "Italian American") population.

History
-------

Morris Park is named after [John Albert Morris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Albert_Morris "John Albert Morris"), who built the [Morris Park Racecourse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Racecourse "Morris Park Racecourse"), which existed from 1889 until 1910.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-live-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-4) In 1890, the Morris Park Racecourse hosted both the [Preakness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preakness_Stakes "Preakness Stakes") and the [Belmont Stakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_Stakes "Belmont Stakes"); the latter continued to be run there until 1905.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-New_York_1_News-5) The track was later used for auto racing and was the site of the first public air show.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-6) After a 1910 fire,[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-7) the property was divided into lots for the current neighborhood. Several streets in Morris Park, including Cruger, Holland, Radcliff, Colden, Paulding, and Hone Avenues, are named after mayors of New York City during the 18th and 19th centuries.

Land use and terrain
--------------------

Housing in Morris Park is mostly one and two family homes of various styles. The neighborhood also has several apartment buildings. The total land area is a little over one-third of a square mile.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-stats-2) The area is low-lying and relatively flat. The northern section of Morris Park nearest [Jacobi Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobi_Medical_Center "Jacobi Medical Center") is also referred to as **Indian Village.** Several streets are named after Native American tribes, including [Choctaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choctaw "Choctaw") Place, [Seminole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seminole "Seminole") Avenue, and [Pawnee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pawnee_people "Pawnee people") Place.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-9)

Demographics
------------

For census purposes, the New York City government classifies Morris Park as part of a larger neighborhood tabulation area called Van Nest/Morris Park/Westchester Square.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-10) Based on data from the [2010 United States Census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_United_States_Census "2010 United States Census"), the population of Van Nest/Morris Park/Westchester Square was 29,250, a change of 2,115 (7.2%) from the 27,135 counted in [2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_United_States_Census "2000 United States Census"). Covering an area of 829.61 acres (335.73 ha), the neighborhood had a population density of 35.3 inhabitants per acre (22,600/sq mi; 8,700/km2).[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-PLP5-11) The racial makeup of the neighborhood was 27.3% (7,987) [White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_/(U.S._Census/) "White (U.S. Census)"), 11.1% (3,245) [African American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_American_/(U.S._Census/) "African American (U.S. Census)"), 0.3% (82) [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_American_/(U.S._Census/) "Native American (U.S. Census)"), 10.6% (3,100) [Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_/(U.S._Census/) "Asian (U.S. Census)"), 0.1% (15) [Pacific Islander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Islander_/(U.S._Census/) "Pacific Islander (U.S. Census)"), 1% (292) from [other races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_/(United_States_Census/) "Race (United States Census)"), and 1.4% (410) from two or more races. [Hispanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic_/(U.S._Census/) "Hispanic (U.S. Census)") or [Latino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latino_/(U.S._Census/) "Latino (U.S. Census)") of any race were 48.3% (14,119) of the population.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-PLP3A-12)

The entirety of Community District 11, which comprises Morris Park and Allerton, had 116,180 inhabitants as of [NYC Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Department_of_Health_and_Mental_Hygiene "New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene")'s 2018 Community Health Profile, with an average life expectancy of 79.9 years.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-CHP2018-13):2, 20 This is lower than the median life expectancy of 81.2 for all New York City neighborhoods.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-:21-14):53 (PDF p. 84)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-15) Most inhabitants are youth and middle-aged adults: 22% are between the ages of between 0–17, 30% between 25–44, and 24% between 45–64. The ratio of college-aged and elderly residents was lower, at 9% and 14% respectively.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-CHP2018-13):2

As of 2017, the median [household income](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Household_income "Household income") in Community District 11 was $48,018.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-CB11PUMA-16) In 2018, an estimated 21% of Morris Park and Allerton residents lived in poverty, compared to 25% in all of the Bronx and 20% in all of New York City. One in eight residents (12%) were unemployed, compared to 13% in the Bronx and 9% in New York City. Rent burden, or the percentage of residents who have difficulty paying their rent, is 55% in Morris Park and Allerton, compared to the boroughwide and citywide rates of 58% and 51% respectively. Based on this calculation, as of 2018, Morris Park and Allerton are considered high-income relative to the rest of the city and not [gentrifying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentrification "Gentrification").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-CHP2018-13):7

Culture
-------

The neighborhood has a large [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italians "Italians") population, and since the early 2000s, has also had a large [Albanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albanians "Albanians") population and smaller Asian and Hispanic neighborhoods.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-:0-17)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-:1-18) Formerly, Morris Park was predominantly Jewish.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-:1-18) It is generally more suburban than other neighborhoods in the Bronx.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-:0-17)

As an Italian American neighborhood, the residents have close ties to their heritage.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-wsj20140404-19) After [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy_national_football_team "Italy national football team")’s [World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA_World_Cup "FIFA World Cup") victory in [2006](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_FIFA_World_Cup "2006 FIFA World Cup"), over 30,000 flocked to the neighborhood for an all-day party. Since then, Morris Park has gained a rival reputation with [Arthur Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Avenue "Arthur Avenue") for the prototypical Italian-American neighborhood in the Bronx. Morris Park has one of the highest percentage of Italian populations in the city, along with [Bensonhurst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bensonhurst "Bensonhurst") in [Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn "Brooklyn") and [Staten Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staten_Island "Staten Island").[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-20)

Morris Park is famous for its annual [Columbus Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Day "Columbus Day") parade, which began in 1977 to honor [Christopher Columbus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Columbus "Christopher Columbus"). It is held on the Sunday before the national Columbus Day holiday. [Rudolph Giuliani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolph_Giuliani "Rudolph Giuliani"), [Michael Bloomberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Bloomberg "Michael Bloomberg"), and [Bill DeBlasio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_DeBlasio "Bill DeBlasio") have attended as mayors.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-21)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-22)[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-23) The procession begins at the intersection of Morris Park Avenue and White Plains Road, marches east on Morris Park Avenue, turns north on Williamsbridge Road, and ends at Pelham Parkway South. The reviewing stand, where the local dignitaries, politicians, civic and business leaders, and [Grand Marshal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Marshal "Grand Marshal") sit, is located on Williamsbridge Road between Lydig and Neill avenues. Past Grand Marshals have included actors [Tony LoBianco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_LoBianco "Tony LoBianco"), [Chazz Palminteri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chazz_Palminteri "Chazz Palminteri"), television personality [Regis Philbin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regis_Philbin "Regis Philbin"), and former [New York Yankees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Yankees "New York Yankees") first baseman [Joe Pepitone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Pepitone "Joe Pepitone").

Politics
--------

Politically, Morris Park is in [New York's 14th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York%27s_14th_congressional_district "New York's 14th congressional district"),[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-24)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-25) represented by Democrat [Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandria_Ocasio-Cortez "Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez") as of 2019.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-26) It is also part of the 34th [State Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State_Senate "New York State Senate") district,[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-27)[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-28) represented by Democrat Nathalia Fernandez and the 80th [State Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State_Assembly "New York State Assembly") district,[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-30)[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-31) represented by Democrat John Zaccaro Jr..[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-32) Morris Park is located in New York's 13th [City Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Council "New York City Council") district, represented by Marjorie Velazquez, a Democrat.

A reflection of its heavily Italian-American and Catholic population, Morris Park was politically conservative and remained one of the Bronx's few solidly [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_/(United_States/) "Republican Party (United States)") neighborhoods until the 1990s.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx#cite_note-wsj20140404-19) It was represented in the [United States Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress") from 1953 to 1969 by [Paul Fino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Fino "Paul Fino"), a Republican, and then from 1969 to 1988 by [Mario Biaggi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Biaggi "Mario Biaggi"), a socially conservative and law and order [Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_/(United_States/) "Democratic Party (United States)"). Republican [State Senators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State_Senate "New York State Senate") such as [John D. Calandra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_D._Calandra "John D. Calandra") and [Guy Velella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guy_Velella "Guy Velella") drew extensive support from Morris Park residents. In his three mayoral campaigns in 1989, 1993, and 1997, [Rudy Giuliani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudy_Giuliani "Rudy Giuliani"), a Republican, carried Morris Park by substantial margins. In recent years, changing demographics have altered the neighborhood's political landscape.

Archivist hopes Morris Park will honor its aviation history
===========================================================

By Ben Kochman Posted on [June 10, 2014](https://www.bxtimes.com/archivist-hopes-morris-park-will-honor-its-aviation-history/)

![Image 7: Archivist hopes Morris Park will honor its aviation history|Archivist hopes Morris Park will honor its aviation history|Archivist hopes Morris Park will honor its aviation history](https://www.bxtimes.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/06/21-airport-2014-05-22-bx01_z.jpg?quality=51&w=500)

Photo by Ben Kochman||

The old Morris park racetrack is famous – but how about some love for the Morris Park Aerodrome?

A local historian hopes his efforts to recognize his hometown’s unique aviation past will get off the ground.

Morris Park is well known for its namesake racetrack, which hosted the Belmont Stakes from the mid-19th century until 1904. But an archivist at Fordham Prep has tracked down evidence that the east Bronx neighborhood was once also home to some of the world’s first glimpses of flying machines.

**First helicopter flight**

“There’s very little of Morris Park history that we celebrate and put out on public display, “ said Louis DiGiorno, who came across his nabe’s aviation past while researching Fordham Prep alumni, many of whom were pilots. “With something this important, we should think about marking it.”

In 1908, the New York Aeronautical Society rented out the former Morris Park racetrack and invited some of the world’s aviation inventors – including the creator of the helicopter – to try out their flying machines at the site.

“Wilbur H. Kimbull’s heliocopter, upon which he has been working for several years, is being assembled at Morris Park and by the end of the week he expects to be ready to try the ascensional power of the machine,” read a story in the September 7, 1908 New York Times.

The airplanes that made it into the air did not go far. The show’s organizers removed the fences around the old racetrack to create an “unobstructed straightway for a flight of at least one kilometer,” according to the Times.

Some of the machines were able to take off — others just looked very impressive.

“The airplane that won design for best airplane couldn’t even fly,” said borough historian Lloyd Ultan.

**Proposed plaque**

The racetrack burned down a few years later, said Ultan, before the land was auctioned off in 1913 to residential real estate developers.

DiGiorno has proposed a plaque or flag in recognition of the area’s aviation history to Community Board 11.

He’s even got a neighborhood tagline ready:

“Morris park: looking up since 1908.”

9.content:
**DALLAS** - New York City has three major airports that are located outside of Manhattan, namely JFK, Newark (EWR), and LaGuardia (LGA). Today we take a look at three lesser-known airports that once served, or almost served, the big apple.

The world's first officially established airport opened in 1908 on the site of a defunct Morris Park racetrack in the Bronx, but it was torn down for development a few years later, incorporated into the expanding city. In its place, city officials picked a location in south Brooklyn that would become Floyd Bennett Field.

A government siting committee chose the Bronx site as one of six potential airport locations; the other four became LaGuardia, Newark Liberty, JFK, and Teterboro airports. The Wright brothers and other pioneers of aviation frequented the fifth, Governor's Island, which had a runway until the 1960s, but that's for another story.

Although plans for a sizable airport in the New York region had been discussed since 1925, little action was taken until 1927, when Charles Lindbergh's solo transatlantic flight really got things moving.

That year, the Bronx Chamber of Commerce realized it needed to make New York's first municipal airport a reality.

Listen to this article:

![Image 1](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/65c26eeea7cdaa706d97a75c/662fc25eac4fcc5efd04ccaa_Bennettfield22121.jpeg)

Floyd Bennet Field. Photo: Msedwick, [Public Domain](https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=12649418)

### Floyd Bennet Field

Floyd Bennett Field came into existence in 1928 by the pumping of sand from the bottom of Jamaica Bay into the waterways separating Barren Island and a few other islands from the rest of Brooklyn. The airfield is located in southeast Brooklyn's Marine Park neighborhood, close to Jamaica Bay. Prior to being used as a naval air station, the airport served as a hub for general and commercial aviation.

Floyd Bennett, a renowned aviator who led the first aircraft to fly above the North Pole and had imagined an airfield at Barren Island before passing away in 1928, had the airport named in his honor.

It was dedicated on June 26, 1930, and on May 23, 1931, it was formally made available for commercial flights. However, Bennett Field did not see much commercial traffic despite the excellent quality of its facilities and was mostly used for general aviation. Aviators flying to or from Bennett Field set scores of aviation records during the interwar period.

The old flying field, which operated from 1911 to 1916, is now a shopping mall, while the eastern field, which was once an industrial park but is now mostly a retail area with townhouses and the Mall at The Source on the site of the former runway.

During the latter 1930s "Golden Age of Aviation," Floyd Bennett Field served as a home base for numerous illustrious pilots. This resulted from a number of favorable circumstances, including the climate, topography, current infrastructure, and little commercial activity.

Bennett Field served as the starting point or final destination of numerous world or transoceanic record-breaking flights, including 26 such trips and 10 such transcontinental flights.

![Image 2](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/65c26eeea7cdaa706d97a75c/662fc25eac4fcc5efd04cc95_1626px-Floyd_Bennett_Field_aerial_from_north_01_-_white_balanced_9454476975-1024x637.jpeg)

Floyd Bennett Field from the air, 2013. Photo: [Joe Mabel](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/User:Jmabel), [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0), [Link](https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=27881663)

Bennett Field is currently managed by the National Park Service and is a part of the Jamaica Bay Unit of the Gateway National Recreation Area (NPS). The New York City Police Department (NYPD) still uses a portion of the airfield as a helicopter base, and one runway is set aside for hobbyists flying radio-controlled aircraft, despite the fact that it is no longer in use as an active commercial, military, or general aviation airfield.

The United States Coast Guard and United States Navy began to occupy a portion of the airport in the 1930s. On June 2, 1941, Bennett Field joined Naval Air Station New York as a result of the start of World War II.

During WWII, Floyd Bennett Field served as a focal point for naval operations. The airfield served as a Naval Air Reserve station after the war. Bennett Field was last used by the Navy in 1970. However, the Coast Guard continued to use it until 1998 and a reserve facility remained there until 1983.

Bennett Field was to be used for a variety of purposes; however, it wasn't until 1972 that it was decided to incorporate the airport within the Gateway National Recreation Area. In 1974, Floyd Bennett Field reopened as a park.

As one of the largest collections and best examples of commercial aviation architecture from the era, and as a result of the region's significant contributions to general aviation and military aviation during the Interwar period, many of the earliest surviving original structures are included in a historic district listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

![Image 3](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/65c26eeea7cdaa706d97a75c/662fc25eac4fcc5efd04ccc1_Lindbergh_takes_off_from_Roosevelt_Field.v1-1024x766.png)

Nearly a thousand people assembled at Roosevelt Field to see Charles Lindbergh off on his historic flight. Underwood and Underwood. Image Number: SI-77-2701 Credit: National Air and Space Museum Archives, Smithsonian Institution.

### Roosevelt Field

A former NY airport called Roosevelt Field can be found 3.7 kilometers (2.3 miles) east-southeast of Mineola, Long Island, New York. During World War I, the United States Army's Air Service used Hazelhurst Field, also known as the Hempstead Plains Aerodrome, Hempstead Plains Field, or even the Garden City Aerodrome, as a training ground.

It was renamed in 1919 to recognize President Theodore Roosevelt's son Quentin, who died in World War I air combat.

Many important flights in the early days of aviation, notably Charles Lindbergh's solo transatlantic flight in 1927, took off from Roosevelt Field. Other early aviators like Amelia Earhart and Wiley Post also employed it.

Once the property was in civilian hands after the war, the owners divided the remaining land into two distinct zones before selling off pieces along the field's southern boundary. Half of the western section along Clinton Road was taken up by Curtiss Field, a 300-acre airfield built on the original site of Hazelhurst Field.

The remaining area was occupied by Roosevelt Field, which included an east-west packed clay runway about 5000 feet in length on the bluff, seven hangars, a sizable parking ramp close to Curtiss Field, and other structures.

![Image 4](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/65c26eeea7cdaa706d97a75c/662fc25eac4fcc5efd04ccad_Aline_H._Rhonie_American_painter_1909-1963_at_work_on_aviation_mural_at_Roosevelt_Field_Garden_City_New_York-1024x828.jpeg)

Aline Hofheimer (1909–1963) painted a 126-foot fresco representing aviation history in Roosevelt Field, Long Island (c. 1935). Photo: Smithsonian Institution. Public Domain  

On September 21, 1926, René Fonck attempted to launch the Sikorsky S-35 in pursuit of the Orteig Prize, but the aircraft was significantly overweight and stressed the auxiliary landing gear placed to help support the burden, breaking a wheel in the process. Two of the crew members died when the plane, unable to reach lift speed, cartwheeled off the end of the cliff and caught fire.

The Roosevelt Field runway would late be used by Charles Lindbergh to take off aboard the Spirit of St. Louis on his voyage to Paris the following May.

During World War II, the Navy and Army both used Roosevelt Field, which resumed operations as a commercial airport following the war until 1950, when it was purchased by real estate developers. On May 31, 1951, the field was shut down.

![Image 5](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/65c26eeea7cdaa706d97a75c/662fc25eac4fcc5efd04ccb7_coop-city-nyc-untapped-cities-jeff-reuben-42ok.v1-1024x639.png)

Photo: Thomas X. Casey, Public Domain

### The Bronx Airport That Never Was

In August 1927, local business people gathered for the opening ceremony of a new airstrip in the Bronx wetlands. Soon after, a single-engine biplane came in for its first landing, but instead of being met with joy, the accident included a parked automobile on the makeshift runway.

Although nobody was hurt, the failed attempt to create an airport in the Bronx was a bad portent. Many residents of New York City and visitors would be arriving in the eastern Bronx today rather than LaGuardia Airport in northern Queens if everything had gone as planned.

On October 1, 1928, one of the New Jersey locations in the Newark region, which is now known as Newark Liberty International Airport, opened. However, a private company's entry into the competition was set to hamper plans for a New York counterpart.

In 1929, a number of aeronautics companies merged to become the Curtiss-Wright Corporation, which at the time was the largest aviation company in the US.

With more than US$35m in cash on hand, Curtiss-Wright decided to diversify its business beyond the production of aircraft by building an extensive network of airports around the country. The eastern Bronx marshes in New York were a terrific fit and offered good value.

![Image 6](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/65c26eeea7cdaa706d97a75c/662fc25eac4fcc5efd04cc7c_95963895_360W.png)

Image courtesy: The New York Times Archives

As soon as possible, Curtiss-Wright started acquiring lands in the Bronx with the intention of building what a local newspaper called "the world's largest airport on the shore of Eastchester Creek."

A June 5, 1929 Headline from _The New York Times_ read, "$3,000,000 AIRPORT PLANNED IN BRONX; Curtiss Corporation Announces Purchase of Site Adjoining Pelham Bay Park. WORK TO BEGIN SOON Triangular 250-Acre Plot Is Termed Ideal for Sea and Land Planes."

As you might have guessed, the residents of the nearby Village of Pelham Manor did not enjoy the notion of having an airport in their backyard. Despite the village's location in Westchester County, local officials tried to change the zoning regulations to stop the airport's construction.

The airport seemed inescapable until the stock market crash in October 1929. With its property taxes on just one location more than half a million dollars past due by 1936, Curtiss-Wright quickly liquidated its airport subsidiary.

By that point, unsatisfied with the travel time from Brooklyn’s Floyd Bennett Field to Manhattan, New York Mayor Fiorello LaGuardia had shifted his sights to northern Queens. In 1934, he refused to deplane at New Jersey’s Newark Airport because his ticket read “New York.” He called for a new, modern airport closer to Manhattan’s business center. That airport, which now bears his name, opened in 1939.

Featured image: A concrete runway at Floyd Bennett Field. Photo: Ad Meskens, [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0), [Link](https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=19477464)
